author: A Robot
objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from a Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry for common covalent molecules.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and how they affect bond angles.
Apply VSEPR theory to real molecules and compare predicted structures with observed geometries.

modules.moduleName: From Lewis Structure to Steric Number
modules.description: Students identify bonding and lone pairs around a central atom and connect the count to steric number.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Count electron domains around a central atom from a Lewis structure.
Relate steric number to the number of regions of electron density.
Prepare for mapping steric number to electron-domain geometry.
instructions: Observe the Lewis structure and identify the central atom.
Count bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.
Use the total number of electron domains to infer the steric number.

components.text: H2O Lewis structure: 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = steric number 4

clips.changeMeaning: The opening clip introduces the counting task and focuses attention on the central oxygen atom as the basis for VSEPR analysis.
clips.narration: VSEPR begins with a Lewis structure. Count every region of electron density around the central atom: each bond counts as one domain, and each lone pair counts as one domain.

clips.changeMeaning: The electron domains expand apart to visually reinforce the counting of four domains and the steric number concept.
clips.narration: For water, oxygen has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. That gives four electron domains, so the steric number is four.

clips.changeMeaning: The scene concludes by summarizing the steric number and preparing the student for the next module on electron-domain geometry.
clips.narration: Steric number is the key bridge from Lewis structure to three-dimensional shape. A steric number of four leads us to a tetrahedral arrangement of electron domains.

modules.description: Students explore the five basic electron-domain geometries and see how electron pairs arrange themselves to minimize repulsion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the five fundamental electron-domain geometries.
Recognize how electron domains arrange to maximize separation in space.
Match steric number to linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral geometries.
instructions: Watch each arrangement form around the central atom.
Compare the domain count with the resulting geometry.
Notice how the same steric number always gives the same electron-domain geometry.

components.text: Linear → trigonal planar → tetrahedral → trigonal bipyramidal → octahedral

clips.changeMeaning: The introductory clip defines electron-domain geometry and anchors the student at the central atom.
clips.narration: Electron-domain geometry describes the arrangement of all electron groups around the central atom, not just the bonds.

clips.changeMeaning: Two electron domains are displayed opposite each other to show the linear arrangement and its 180-degree separation.
clips.narration: With two domains, the lowest-repulsion arrangement is linear, with the groups directly opposite each other at 180 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: The domains reposition into a tetrahedral arrangement to demonstrate the characteristic 3D separation for steric number four.
clips.narration: Four domains arrange tetrahedrally, with ideal bond angles of about 109.5 degrees. This is the arrangement behind methane and many related molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: The scene reveals the remaining domain counts and their geometries, expanding the student’s map from steric number to shape.
clips.narration: Five domains form a trigonal bipyramidal geometry. Six domains form an octahedral geometry, with the domains spread as far apart as possible in three dimensions.

modules.description: Students compare electron-domain geometry with molecular geometry, then see how lone pairs reshape the observed molecular shape and slightly compress bond angles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Differentiate electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
Identify common shapes produced by lone pairs: bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and square planar.
Explain why lone pairs compress bond angles relative to ideal values.
instructions: Focus on the positions of the atoms, not the lone pairs, when naming molecular geometry.
Watch how lone pairs occupy extra space and distort the bond angles.
Compare the ideal angle with the observed angle shown on screen.

components.text: Molecular geometry ignores lone pairs in the name

clips.changeMeaning: The introductory clip sets up the distinction between counting all domains and naming only atom positions in the molecule.
clips.narration: Electron-domain geometry includes lone pairs. Molecular geometry describes only the positions of the atoms. That distinction matters when lone pairs are present.

clips.changeMeaning: The lone-pair examples are brought forward and annotated to show both the trigonal pyramidal and bent shapes and their compressed bond angles.
clips.narration: Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal because one lone pair occupies one position of a tetrahedral electron arrangement. Water is bent because two lone pairs occupy two positions, leaving only two atoms visible in the molecular shape.

clips.changeMeaning: The final clip emphasizes that lone pairs take up more space than bonding pairs, explaining the smaller-than-ideal bond angles.
clips.narration: Lone pairs are attracted to only one nucleus, so they spread out more and repel other electron domains more strongly than bonding pairs. That extra repulsion compresses bond angles below the ideal values.

modules.description: Students apply VSEPR to several representative molecules and compare predicted shapes with experimentally observed molecular structures.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict the shapes of common molecules from their electron-domain counts.
Match VSEPR predictions to real molecules including methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4.
Recognize how lone pairs change the final molecular geometry while preserving electron-domain geometry.
instructions: Use the molecule cards to identify the steric number and predicted shape.
Compare each predicted geometry with the displayed 3D model.
Notice which molecules are ideal and which are distorted by lone pairs.

components.text: Compare predicted VSEPR shapes to observed structures

clips.changeMeaning: The overview clip introduces the comparison task and frames the molecule cards as concrete applications of the theory.
clips.narration: Now apply VSEPR to real molecules. The same counting rules let us predict shapes for familiar species and compare them with observed structures.

clips.changeMeaning: The first comparison group highlights molecules whose shapes directly match ideal VSEPR geometries without lone-pair distortion.
clips.narration: Methane is tetrahedral. PF5 is trigonal bipyramidal. SF6 is octahedral. In each case, the observed structure closely matches the electron-domain geometry because there are no lone pairs on the central atom.

clips.changeMeaning: XeF4 is brought into focus as the lone-pair-controlled example that becomes square planar even though its electron-domain geometry is octahedral.
clips.narration: XeF4 is the classic lone-pair example. It has six electron domains, so its electron-domain geometry is octahedral, but two of those domains are lone pairs. The molecular geometry is square planar.

clips.changeMeaning: The final clip recaps the overall workflow so students leave with a repeatable method for solving VSEPR problems.
clips.narration: The VSEPR workflow is consistent: count domains, identify electron-domain geometry, remove lone pairs from the name, and then consider how lone pairs compress bond angles. That sequence predicts the three-dimensional structure of many covalent molecules.
